title: Do Generate–Verify–Repair Guards Improve LLM NetOps Outputs? A Paired Emulator Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (n=200 natural-language NetOps intents; preregistration SHA-256 e5c5fdbd717c2c05118643e1d7d5f44055f6356dcf2083bd47c5766cf780ff68) to measure whether a bounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline improves the proportion of emulator-executable configurations versus accepting ungated LLM outputs. Generation used gpt-5-mini with a shared-initial-generation protocol (one candidate per intent shared by both arms). A deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) checked candidates; when violations fell into repairable classes a deterministic rule-based repair operator was permitted ≤1 invocation. Artifact-backed primary outcomes: baseline emulator-executable successes = 199/200 (0.995), guarded = 200/200 (1.000); paired contingency n11=199, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided (binomial) test on discordant pairs (n10+n01) yields p = 1.0; paired-bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.015]. The observed near-ceiling baseline prevents detection of the preregistered 15 percentage-point effect. We (1) describe the validator and deterministic repair operator; (2) report precise execution accounting (400 episodes completed, hosted-model calls used = 201, deterministic repair invocations = 1, provider/API failures = 0); (3) provide exact inference details for small discordant counts; and (4) discuss operational implications, limitations, and reproducibility. All prompts, provider traces, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution and analysis bundles referenced in the evidence manifest.

sections.introduction: Automating routine network-operations (NetOps) tasks with generative large language models (LLMs) can increase efficiency but raises safety and correctness concerns: LLMs may emit configurations that are syntactically plausible but operationally unsafe or incomplete (omitted prerequisites, incorrect ordering, protected-interface modifications). Prior work proposes verifier-assisted and repair architectures to reduce such failures, but there is limited execution-grounded evidence quantifying marginal gains under conservative resource budgets. We preregistered a narrowly scoped paired experiment to measure whether a bounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) guard increases the proportion of emulator-executable configurations relative to accepting ungated LLM outputs. To isolate the deterministic validator/repair operator's capacity, we used a shared-initial-generation estimand: one LLM candidate per intent, produced once and evaluated both as (A) ungated baseline and (B) guarded GVR flow. Our principal contribution is an artifact-backed, preregistered paired evaluation (study_id cnd-001-5f3a) reporting exact paired counts, a concise deterministic-repair algorithmic description, exact small-sample inferential handling for McNemar discordants, and an evidence-grounded discussion of operational implications and limitations.
sections.related_work: Contemporary surveys and prototype studies document active application of LLMs to intent-to-configuration translation, co-pilot assistance, and automated repair proposals. Reports highlight hallucinations and schema violations as recurring failure modes and describe mitigations including constrained decoding, live schema grounding, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), verifier-assisted loops, and tool-augmented correction. Formal-method verifiers (NetKAT variants and ensemble verifiers) can detect reachability and isolation violations but trade off fidelity and scalability. Our work complements these by providing an execution-grounded paired measurement of a bounded, deterministic repair operator applied to an identical LLM candidate—an estimand that isolates whether deterministic, rule-based repair can recover validator-failing candidates without additional LLM resampling.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental plan: The study was preregistered and frozen before execution (preregistration SHA-256 e5c5fdbd...ff68). Confirmatory set: n=200 natural-language change intents curated to span single-device and small multi-device changes (ACLs, VLAN/MTU updates, uplink switchover patterns). Design and estimand: shared-initial-generation with a paired binary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Model and budget: declared model gpt-5-mini; planned max hosted-model calls = 400; realized model calls = 201. Execution environment and validator: a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator was orchestrated by adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the deterministic validator used is deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Outcome definition: a successful episode is one where the validator reports validation_after.valid == true after applying the candidate (with repairs applied in the guarded arm when permitted). Missingness and retries: per preregistration, transient provider/API errors received a single automatic retry; provider/API failures would be counted as failures in primary analysis. All artifact paths, hashes and logs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis bundle.
sections.results: Execution accounting and raw outcomes (artifact-backed): all planned episodes completed (400 episodes = 200 pairs) with zero provider/API failures; hosted-model calls used = 201 (shared_initial_generation = 200, repair stage calls = 1). Primary outcome counts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): baseline successes = 199/200 (0.995), guarded successes = 200/200 (1.000). Paired contingency: n11 = 199 (both arms success), n10 = 1 (guarded success only), n01 = 0 (baseline success only), n00 = 0 (both fail). Deterministic repair accounting: initial validator failures (validation_before.valid == false) occurred in exactly 1 episode; deterministic repair invocations = 1; syntactic parse failures = 0. The single repair converted the validator-failing candidate into a validator-passing configuration (archived repair trace available in the evidence bundle). Statistical inference—exact McNemar implementation: the preregistered primary test uses the exact McNemar formulation appropriate for small discordant counts by treating the count of discordant pairs in one direction (n10) as Binomial(n = n10 + n01, p = 0.5) under the null. Observed discordants: n10 = 1, n01 = 0, so n = 1 and the two-sided exact binomial test yields p = 1.0 (artifact: analysis/results.json). Complementary uncertainty quantification used a paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples and seed 1729, yielding [0.0, 0.015] (artifact: analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The bootstrap CI therefore excludes the preregistered detectable effect of 0.15 due to the realized near-ceiling baseline. Secondary analyses: predeclared secondary estimands (repair-iteration counts, proportion of verifier-detected faults corrected by repairs, failure-taxonomy distribution) were constrained by the single repair event and are reported descriptively in archived CSVs rather than as inferential findings.
sections.discussion: Estimator interpretation and operational implications: the shared-initial-generation estimand isolates deterministic repair-on-same-candidate efficacy but does not evaluate designs that permit independent resampling or iterated LLM repairs. For the curated confirmatory distribution and resource-conservative budget (repair budget ≤1, single shared candidate), the deterministic repair operator provided a marginal absolute gain of 0.5 percentage points (1/200). Practical takeaways: (1) deterministic validators serve as effective assurance gates and provide actionable diagnostic violation codes that enable automated repairs or human escalation; (2) when baseline LLM generation quality is near-ceiling, bounded deterministic repair-on-same-candidate yields negligible marginal improvement; (3) in harder task distributions or under an independent-resampling estimand, verifier-assisted designs that allow additional LLM calls or larger repair budgets could provide larger operational gains at the cost of greater model-call expenditure. Validator and repair semantics (concise, artifact-grounded description): the validator performs three logical stages—(a) syntactic parse and normalization of CLI-like lines into canonical tokens and a normalized_configuration string; (b) structural and workflow checks enforcing required-command presence, dependency/make-before-break patterns, group/activity constraints, and protected-interface checks; (c) deterministic final-state simulation applying the normalized configuration to the emulator model and comparing observed final_state fields to the task’s expected_final_state. Violation-code families logged include SYNTAX_PARSE_ERROR, MISSING_REQUIRED_COMMAND, DEPENDENCY_VIOLATION, PROTECTED_INTERFACE_MODIFICATION, FINAL_STATE_MISMATCH, and TRANSIENT_RULE_VIOLATION. Deterministic repair operator (algorithmic summary): the guarded pipeline invoked an internal, deterministic repair operator only when the validator returned violation_count>0 and the violations belonged to repairable classes (primarily MISSING_REQUIRED_COMMAND and DEPENDENCY_VIOLATION). The operator performs rule-based, non-ML transformations to the normalized_configuration: (1) insert validator-identified missing commands (for example, explicit shutdown or restore commands identified as required by the workflow policy), (2) reorder command blocks to satisfy dependency constraints (make-before-break patterns), and (3) preserve protected-interface statements and unspecified state per task constraints. Repair invocation rule: repair is deterministically applied at most once per episode (bounded repair budget ≤1) and only for violations matched to the operator’s repairable families; repaired configurations are re-validated by the same deterministic validator. Robustness and threats to validity: internal validity concerns include prompt sensitivity limited to a single model and the shared-generation choice, which isolates repair but does not evaluate independent-resampling designs; construct validity concerns include emulator and validator fidelity—Dockerized Mininet+FRR and the deterministic validator model control-plane behavior deterministically but do not capture all production dynamics (e.g., asynchronous BGP convergence timing, vendor-specific CLI idiosyncrasies); external validity concerns include single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and a synthetic curated task set that may not represent broad production heterogeneity. Reproducibility and artifacts: all prompts, provider-call traces, responses, validator traces, repair traces (the single invoked repair), analysis CSVs and logs, and the full execution manifest are archived in the evidence bundle referenced by the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*). The preregistration SHA is provided above; analysis artifacts record bootstrap parameters (seed 1729, 10,000 resamples) and the exact McNemar implementation used. Reviewer-requested per-task difficulty counts: per-task difficulty metadata (easy/medium/hard/very_hard) are recorded for every confirmatory intent in execution/task_manifest.jsonl; these per-episode difficulty annotations are available in the archived task manifest and may be inspected directly in the evidence bundle. The present confirmatory manuscript does not invent or summarize numeric difficulty counts beyond representative examples; researchers and practitioners can extract exact counts from the archived manifest (manifest hash recorded in the execution manifest) for context-sensitive interpretation.
sections.conclusion: We executed an autonomy-locked, preregistered paired experiment to evaluate a bounded generate–verify–repair guard for LLM-generated NetOps configurations under a shared-initial-generation estimand. Ungated gpt-5-mini generation succeeded in 199/200 confirmatory cases; the GVR pipeline succeeded in 200/200. The artifact-backed paired difference = 0.005 (exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.015]), which excludes the preregistered 15 percentage-point target effect due to a realized near-ceiling baseline. For the studied distribution and estimand, deterministic repair-on-same-candidate yielded a negligible marginal improvement; broader operational value depends on task hardness, estimand choice (shared-candidate vs independent-resampling), model capability, repair budget, and emulator fidelity. Future work should evaluate independent-resampling guarded designs, multivendor CLI diversity, adversarial/out-of-distribution intents, larger repair budgets, and improved emulator fidelity to better characterize when GVR guards provide substantive operational benefits.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock defined by the initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human involvement prior to the lock was limited to selecting the topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and approving the master prompt and autonomy boundary. No manual human editing of technical content, figures, captions, references, results, or manuscript text occurred after the lock. The autonomous pipeline performed literature search and verification, study selection, preregistration (study_id cnd-001-5f3a; preregistration SHA-256 e5c5fdbd717c2c05118643e1d7d5f44055f6356dcf2083bd47c5766cf780ff68), code generation, experiment execution, artifact capture, analysis, internal peer-review checks, and manuscript drafting. Models and tooling: generation used gpt-5-mini (provider recorded in execution/model_configuration.json); validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (scorer_id/scorer_version and scoring_rule 'full_intent_constraint_validation' are recorded in scoring artifacts); execution used a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator orchestrated by adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Key preregistered settings (not altered post-lock): primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; confirmatory sample n=200 paired intents; maximum model-call budget = 400; repair budget ≤1 deterministic repair iteration; analysis plan = exact McNemar two-sided with paired bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Execution accounting (artifact-backed): the run completed 400 episodes (200 pairs) using 201 hosted-model calls; provider-call stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=200, repair=1. All prompts, provider-call traces, responses, validator traces, repair traces (the single invoked repair), analysis artifacts, and the full execution manifest are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in the manuscript (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*).
limitations: Synthetic, curated task set focused on small single- and multi-device changes; not comprehensive of production NetOps workloads (multivendor CLIs, hardware idiosyncrasies, dynamic control-plane timing).
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) evaluated; findings do not imply multi-model generality.

Emulator (Dockerized Mininet+FRR) and deterministic validator model control-plane behavior but do not fully capture production runtime dynamics such as BGP convergence timing or vendor-specific runtime effects.
Preregistered repair budget limited to a single deterministic repair iteration in the confirmatory protocol; different repair strategies or additional iterations might yield different outcomes.

Shared-initial-generation design (single initial candidate per intent shared across arms) reduced model-call cost and isolated repair effectiveness on identical candidates but reduces external generalizability compared with independent re-sampling per arm.
Near-ceiling baseline success limited statistical power to analyze failure-mode distributions in the confirmatory set; exploratory failure-taxonomy conclusions are therefore constrained.
Adversarial or out-of-distribution intents (e.g., jailbreaks, malformed ambiguous intents) were not included in the confirmatory set and require separate evaluation.

Aggregate per-intent difficulty annotations (easy / medium / hard / very_hard) for all 200 confirmatory intents are recorded in the archived task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; manifest hash is recorded in the execution manifest) and are available in the evidence bundle for per-task inspection; the manuscript does not invent numeric counts that are not already present in archived artifacts.
